 By Andrew Chesterton Updated October 26 2026 - 4:03pm , first published 11:00am By Andrew Chesterton Updated October 26 2026 - 4:03pm , first published 11:00am Save Share Mitsubishi Pajero 2026 review: Australian first drive | Likes
 Comfortable, plush cabin 
 Modern and fresh-feeling tech 
 Looks great in the metal 
 Dislikes
 Third-row ergonomic quirks 
 Low-res off-road cameras 
 On-road performance still a mystery 
 This might sound a little mean, and I really don't mean it to, but the new Mitsubishi Pajero is, quite literally, shockingly good when you meet it in person. Shocking because, on paper, it had begun to sound a little like another Mitsubishi roll-the-arm-over special.
 A platform borrowed from the Mitsubishi Triton , an engine borrowed from the same ute , which was itself borrowed from the previous Triton, such is its vintage. And all from a brand without a known passion for the latest in cabin materials and technology .
 So it's a relief to finally encounter the Pajero in person and to discover that any misgivings are unwarranted. On first impressions, at least, this feels like a true return to form for Mitsubishi , and for the iconic Pajero nameplate.
 Read more

 2027 Mitsubishi Pajero 'Shorty' could be Australia's coolest new 4WD, and an answer to Toyota FJ LandCruiser, Suzuki Jimny 
 2026 Mitsubishi Pajero faces real battle against Toyota Prado, Ford Everest and Isuzu MU-X 4WDs, and this is what it needs to get right | Opinion 
 Modern-feeling and user-friendly tech
 Granted, all of our time was spent in the top-spec GSR grade ($84,990), which sports the best stuff, including 20-inch black alloy wheels and the very nice two-tone camel-and-black leather trim, but even the cheapest GLS grade ($68,490) gets plenty of high-tech stuff, including twin 12.3-inch displays and a 12.3-inch driver display. All get an underbody-mounted spare wheel, too.
 On the price for a second, whether that's a bargain or not depends on how you see the Pajero. It's less than something like a Toyota Prado , but more than other ute-based SUVs like the Ford Everest or Isuzu MU-X .
 + 5 This isn't an ASX time machine, and nor is it a warmed-over Triton with an SUV body. It feels genuinely fresh, new and modern, and it might just be the best vehicle the brand has launched in years.
 To know for sure, we'll have to wait for the official launch later this year, but after our brief off-road sample, the signs are looking good.
 Pajero - old versus new
 Mitsubishi made the deviously ingenious decision to have us lap the same off-road circuit twice - once behind the wheel of the old Pajero, and once driving the new one - and the difference was staggering.
 I liken it to a bit like mobile phones. The first Pajero is a clunky Blackberry, and the new one is an iPhone 18, both will perform the same basic tasks - calls, texts, emails - but the way they achieve those goals is starkly different. 
 The first Pajero remains capable, but it is a rough, rugged donkey ride up the side of a mountain. The new one, with its clever traction and off-road brain, feels massively more comfortable and luxurious, with the suspension able to soak up so much more punishment before bouncing its occupants around the cabin. The steering, too, feels far more switched-on and responsive, with fewer lock-to-lock turns and far more engagement.
 + 8 It's as about as comfortable as it gets in the bone-punishing world of off-roading, and I would argue a damn site more pleasant than most dual-cab utes, including the Triton. Off-road purists might stare at you through their beards and tell you that there's something charming, romantic even, about a rough-and-ready analogue 4WD that's now missing from the modern Pajero. But these people like sleeping outside even after the invention of the flushing toilet, and so are not to be listened to.
 We know already that Mitsubishi has dodged electrification entirely for Pajero, and instead fitted a 2.4-litre single-turbo-diesel four-cylinder engine making 150kW and 480Nm. Despite calling it newly developed, the engine actually dates back to the Triton before the current Triton. There's a new eight-speed automatic on board, too, and the prerequisite 3.5-tonne towing capacity, along with a fuel use promise of around 7.0 litres per hundred kays.
 Is that enough power to shift a vehicle this big on a freeway overtake? I have no idea, to be honest. I don't think I cracked 20km/h on the off-road circuit. Still, the grunt didn't underwhelm.
 + 7 The Pajero sports Mitsi's off-road tech, like Super Select 4WD with 4 High and 4 Low with a centre diff lock, along with a separate switch for the rear diff lock, but the track we were on wasn't challenging enough for us to use all of them. Still, there were places where Pajero old and new both struggled for grip, and the new one found traction sooner, and with less fuss in the cabin.
 At 4920mm long, 1925mm wide and 1910mm tall, it's a big unit, and it feels it off-road, where obstacles feel close to the expensive bits of the metal. Helping mitigate that somewhat is the off-road camera that shows you what's happening outside the car, but that seems to be the only piece of technology that's been teleported from the past, with the image blurry and underwhelming.
 2026 Mitsubishi Pajero GSR How is the space in all three rows?
 Like the mid-grade Exceed, our test GSR is a seven-seat only proposition (though you can opt for five seats in the entry-level GLS), and space in the second row is both ample and comfortable. The seatbacks of the two front seats are home to USB-C charging ports, and there's a home-style power point between them, which is a great addition, and one you usually only find in electrified vehicles. There's also rear seat heating in the window seats, and climate settings, too. See what I mean about this feeling more modern than most Mitsubishis?
 There is a bit of weirdness in the third row, though. Getting in is easy enough - you pull a level and the seat folds flat and forwards, making it easy for my 175cm frame to climb in. Once in though, there are raised portions on the floor of both sides of the cabin, making it impossible to sit with both feet flat and even on the floor, so you end up tilting towards the centre. Adults will hate it, though kids can sit back there easily enough.
 And kudos to Mitsubishi for blending old and new all over the cabin, and for displaying a real attention to detail, too. The big screens are joined by physical controls for the air-con and volume, for example, and I love the way 'Pajero' has been hot-stamped into the leather in places like on the grab handles.
 + 5 So yes, shockingly good so far. The real test still awaits, but this is looking good for Mitsubishi. Add a 10-year (conditional) warranty and 10 years of capped-price servicing , and the brand could be onto a winner.
 Verdict
 The real Pajero story will be revealed later this year, but it's impressive so far. It feels new, fresh and - most importantly - complete. Mitsubishi is clearly taking this seriously, and it doesn't feel as though it has cut any corners.
 Note: CarsGuide attended this event as a guest of the manufacturer with travel, accommodation and meals provided.
